meta.title: Starting the Cold Engine
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses vivid verbs that make a mechanical step clear to picture.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 136w at FK 5.7, part_2 114w at FK 7.0, part_3 126w at FK 6.7. The load is vivid verbs and the order of a cold start.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Ford Motor Company, Ford Manual for Owners and Operators of Ford Cars and Trucks (1919), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Ford Motor Company. Ford Manual for Owners and Operators of Ford Cars and Trucks. 1919. Project Gutenberg eBook #46206, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/46206, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: The authoring pass split long sentences, simplified technical nouns to their function, and kept the source's safety caution; no facts added.
source.survey: A 1919 Ford manual shows a driver how to work the starting crank by hand and then gives the numbered steps for starting the engine on a cold day.
source.drafted_by: LessonBot harness (DeepSeek 1017), adapted from the human source; source review completed

session.difficulty_basis: vivid verbs that make a mechanical step clear to picture

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: If the car has no built-in start, start the engine by moving the crank up at the front of the car. Take hold of the handle and push firmly toward the car until you feel the crank catch, then lift upward with a quick swing. When the engine is cool, prime the carb by a short pull on the small wire at the lower left front while giving the engine two or three quarter turns with the crank handle. To start a cold engine, turn the carb dash knob a fourth of a turn left. This lets a richer mix into the engine. Then hold out the prime rod and turn the crank six to eight one-quarter turns in a row. Or turn the motor over a few times with the built-in start.
passage.part_2: A different way to start a hard-to-start cold engine is this: before you throw on the spark switch, (1) close the gas lever. (2) hold out the prime rod while you give the crank a few quick turns, or turn the motor over a few times with the starter, then let go of the prime rod, making sure it goes back all the way. (3) place the spark lever in about the third notch and move the gas lever up a few notches. (4) throw on the switch, making sure to get it on the side marked for spark. (5) give the crank one or two turns, or close the start switch, and the motor should start.
passage.part_3: After you start the motor, it is best to move the spark up eight or ten marks on the lever and let the motor go until it is fully hot. If you start with a cold motor, you will not have much power and may stall. The good thing about putting the switch on last, or after feeding gas first, is that when you throw on the switch and start the motor, you have plenty of gas in the engine to keep the motor going. This does away with the bother of the motor going on and off. After the motor is warmed up, move the carb knob back one-fourth turn. Careful: do not move the spark too far, or the engine may kick back.

items.prompt: In the opening, how far does the passage say to turn the carb dash knob to start a cold engine?

tutor_only.confirm: Turn the carb dash knob a fourth of a turn left.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'To start a cold engine, turn the carb dash knob a fourth of a turn left.' states the exact amount and direction.
tutor_only.tell: Turn the carb dash knob a fourth of a turn left.
help: Reread the sentence that begins 'To start a cold engine.'
Look for the fraction and the direction in that sentence.
tutor_only.core_idea: For a cold engine, the carb dash knob turns a fourth of a turn left.
accept_ideas: a fourth of a turn left
one quarter turn to the left
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the knob turns all the way left.
if_they_say.ask: What fraction does the passage give for that turn?

items.prompt: The carb knob goes left before the crank turns. What does that order tell you a cold engine needs?

tutor_only.confirm: Fuel in the cylinder before the cranking — the turns only work once the richer mix is in.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The answer comes from the sentences 'To start a cold engine, turn the carb dash knob a fourth of a turn left. This lets a richer mix into the engine. Then hold out the prime rod and turn the crank six to eight quick turns of a fourth each in a row.'
tutor_only.tell: The knob goes left first to send in a richer mix. Then the quick turns can start the cold engine.
help: Name the step that adds a richer mix.
Name the step that turns the crank.
tutor_only.core_idea: The order shows the cold engine needs a richer mix before the cranking can start it.
accept_ideas: A richer mix before the cranking.
Fuel in the engine before the crank turns.
The carb knob must go left first.
The engine needs gas before it will catch.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the order does not matter.
if_they_say.ask: What does the knob do before the crank turns?

items.prompt: The passage puts the spark switch on last. Why would the writer save the switch for last?

tutor_only.confirm: The engine already has gas when the spark arrives. Switching on first gives a dry start.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Steps 1–3 prime the engine and set the gas and spark levers before step 4 throws on the spark switch.
tutor_only.tell: The switch goes on last so gas is already in the engine. If the spark comes first, the motor may start and stop.
help: Look at what steps 1 through 3 do before step 4.
Think about what the engine needs before the spark switch is thrown.
tutor_only.core_idea: The switch goes on last so the engine already has gas when the spark arrives.
accept_ideas: So the engine has gas before the spark.
The gas must be in the engine first.
A dry start makes the motor stop and start.
The fuel needs to be ready before the spark.
not_required: whether the crank or starter is used
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the switch should go on first.
if_they_say.ask: What does the engine need before the spark arrives?

items.prompt: The crank will 'catch,' then you 'lift upward with a quick swing.' What do the two verbs show?

tutor_only.confirm: Two stages: the catch as it engages, then the quick arc of the swing.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence says to push until you feel the crank 'catch,' then 'lift upward with a quick swing,' so the two verbs split one pull into an engage and an arc.
tutor_only.tell: 'Catch' is the moment it engages. 'Swing' is the quick arc of the pull.
help: Find the words 'catch' and 'swing' in the crank sentence.
Name what each word does in the pull.
tutor_only.core_idea: First it catches, then the big swing.
accept_ideas: first it catches, then the big swing
the verbs split the pull into a grab and an arc
the crank catches and then swings up
not_required: explaining what a spark switch is
saying it means turn on the switch
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the verbs only mean 'turn the crank.'
if_they_say.ask: What do 'catch' and 'swing' each do in the pull?

partial.when: the student describes a general picture of starting an old car, or says the verbs only mean how to start it
partial.ask: What do the words 'catch' and 'swing' show about the pull itself?

tutor_only.full_idea: 'Catch' is the moment the crank engages; 'swing' is the quick arc of the pull, so the two verbs split one action into stages.

items.prompt: The opening gives start-up steps. What does the writer start doing in the last part?

tutor_only.confirm: The writer moves from giving start-up steps to explaining why the order works and what to do after starting.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part 1's 'If the car has no built-in start...' gives start-up steps; part 3's 'After you start the motor...' gives after-start warming, and 'The good thing about putting the switch on last...' explains why the order helps.
tutor_only.tell: The opening gives steps. The last part explains the reason for the order and how to warm the motor.
help: The opening gives steps for getting the engine going.
The last part explains why the order helps and what to do after it starts.
tutor_only.core_idea: The last part explains why the order works and gives after-start warming advice.
accept_ideas: It explains why the order works.
It gives advice for after the start.
It tells how to warm the motor.
It moves from steps to reasons and warming.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the last part repeats the steps.
if_they_say.ask: What does the last part explain that the opening does not?

partial.when: The student names a control, such as the spark or the carb, without saying the writer has moved from steps to reasons and warming.
partial.ask: The opening lists steps. What kind of writing does the last part add?
